newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Berlusconi hopes for swift trial restart.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Berlusconi hopes for swift trial restart.

text.p: The year-old corruption trial of Italy's former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi was thrown into disarray on Monday when the presiding judge stepped down in a row over allegations of bias.
The decision by judge Carlo Crivelli meant the trial in Milan, at which Berlusconi and 10 others are charged with complicity in corruption, might have to re-start from scratch.

"At this point, all that concerns us is that the trial begins again as soon as possible in a climate as calm as that in other Milanese courts in which the accused are presumed innocent just as the constitution says," Berlucsoni's lawyers Ennio Amodio and Giuseppe De Luca said in a statement.
Crivelli's decision was one of a brace of courtroom twists in cases involving the Berlusconi family on Monday.

In the northern town of Brescia, the prosecution asked a separate trial to acquit Berlusconi's brother Paolo and three co-defendants accused of plotting to force former star anti-graft magistrate Antonio Di Pietro to resign.
Prosecutor Raimondo Giustozzi, who took over the case mid-way through proceedings, said there was no evidence to support charges of extortion against the four men.

The two cases are loosely connected since Di Pietro was the star of the "Clean Hands" team of magistrates which led investigations in 1994 into the alleged payment of bribes to tax police by companies in Berlusconi's media empire.
He quit as a magistrate shortly after the team sought to indict Berlusconi but has never fully explained his reasons.
Crivelli's resignation followed an attempt by Silvio and Paolo Berlusconi and two other defendants last October to have him removed from the bench on grounds of partiality.
Their application was based on a private exchange between the presiding judge Crivelli and a prosecutor in which Crivelli spoke of a "carrot and stick" approach to the trial.
A court of appeal rejected the suit but ruled that the remark, picked up on court microphones but outside formal court proceedings, showed a "serious lapse of style".

In a written statement to the court, Crivelli said the appeal court ruling had undermined his public prestige and allowed the defendants who had challenged his impartiality "to avoid their natural judge and alter the duration of the trial".
Proceedings were adjourned until February 5 pending the appointment of a new judge but defence lawyers vowed to press for the trial, which opened on January 17 1996, to begin afresh.

Berlusconi, who leads the opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance, denies charges that he and others in his Fininvest business empire paid bribes to tax inspectors between 1989 and 1991 to obtain favourable audits.
He has portrayed the trial, and a separate case in which he is charged with false accounting and illegal political party financing, as a plot by magistrates to ruin him politically.
Berlusconi's legal woes began while he was prime minister in 1994 when Di Pietro and the "Clean Hands" team he spearheaded undertook a flurry of investigations into his business affairs.
The theory that Berlusconi's supporters hit back by seeking to discredit Di Pietro appeared to evaporate on Monday with Giustozzi's request for acquittal at the Brescia trial.
A verdict in that case, which involves Paolo Berlusconi, former defence minister Cesare Previti and two former justice ministry inspectors, is expected this week.
